doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Opening and Kansas City head arrangements
title: Explaining the head arrangement and the gospel preacher model
summary: Jimmy explains head arrangements in the Kansas City style; Jeannie ties the build of solos to the preacher and congregation of gospel.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well for some of our maybe — students that will watch this later on, you said you know, that was a head arrangement.
Yeah, totally.
Could you just, in your own words, explain about the head arrangement? Because that’s a bit of a lost art these days.

Oh, yeah. Well one of the main reasons is due to the times, you know, because coming up in our era, and all the perennial giants who set the pace for everything you know, they did a lot of head playing, and specifically noted for that was the Kansas City style see? That’s why we refer to the Kansas City style. In other words, riffs, tunes, and you make up a tune and you take it until you decide to—
To stop.

To stop. It could be all night. Really. Depends on the groove you know and everything. And so in other words, it just comes immediately, it’s an improvisation right from — a spontaneous phrase right from the get-go, you know, from the head. And everybody’s just tuning in to each other you know. While one is playing the lead, another will set up a tune, and they listen to it and make a little background to it or something like that. Or they’ll pick up the tune as a total unison thing, and make it a big mass unison, and then go into solos and then riffs and things like that.
And then it might get written down later.
Oh, yeah, later. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Yeah, especially if they like it. I think also that it’s best to be taken from like Gospel or spiritual music you know? Because you always have a lead singer, or the preacher, he’s doing his thing and everybody’s saying “Amen.” And then the preacher goes from the one to the third to the fifth to the seventh. And when he hits the seventh he’s ready to take everybody out.
Yeah. That’s how you get this going.

Yeah, I noted that even when I was little. And so whoever is playing the solo is the preacher for the moment. And everybody else is doing “Amen.” And then the next soloist takes over, and he’s the preacher for the moment, and everybody else says the “Amen.” So it’s really that simple.
Really.
But you’ve got to live it.
He’d follow — and soloists would follow that, would actually follow that format, in terms like she was saying, tonic, third, fifth, seventh. That’s why each chorus —
Sort of grows.
Grows.
And it changes.
In other words you become aware of building. Like creativity. Like the law of creativity dictates that. In terms of the energy. Energizing.
And when you got up to that seventh, that just kind of had to resolve eventually?
Eventually.
Eventually. Sometimes you’d just leave it hanging you see? So that’s why you start having dominant chord endings, see?
Oh. Come back next week and we’ll find it.
We’ll find it.
